newsitem.title: UK: New Greenpeace campaign takes aim at Atlantic oil.
newsitem.headline: New Greenpeace campaign takes aim at Atlantic oil.

text.p: Environmental group Greenpeace on Wednesday launched a high-profile campaign to shore up public opposition to big oil developments in deep Atlantic waters off the British coast.

At a solar-powered presentation in a London theatre, Greenpeace Executive Director Peter Melchett said: "This campaign is designed to protect the climate...by engaging with a solid, real target which is the linchpin of the problem - that is the exploration end of the oil industry. And with an equally real, solid solution -- and that is solar power."

The campaign includes a short film to be shown in cinemas across Britain, a new internet site, a petition aimed at the new British Prime Minister Tony Blair and a high-street tour of a mobile solar-powered kitchen.

Oil companies discovered commercial quantities of oil in the Atlantic frontier west of the Shetland islands five years ago and first flows from British Petroleum's Foinaven field are expected this summer.
Greenpeace said that fossil fuels must remain in the ground if carbon dioxde emissions that cause global warming are to be curbed.
"For the sake of the climate, this is a frontier too far," said Greenpeace campaigner Sarah Burton.
The environmental group is also concerned about the impact of oil drilling on marine wildlife.
"The Atlantic frontier is not just swarming with oil men looking for oil, it is swarming with birds, sea-life and whales," Burton said.
In 1995, Greenpeace forced Anglo-Dutch oil giant Shell to rethink its plans to ditch the Brent spar platform at sea.
A high-profile campaign involved Greenpeace attempts to block the platform being towed to its Atlantic dumping site and a boycott of Shell petrol stations in Europe.
Campaigners would not be drawn on whether similar direct action was planned in the Atlantic frontier, but a Greenpeace ship is already in the area, they said.
"One lesson we learnt from Brent Spar is that working together with the public...groups like Greenpeace stand a chance of changing the minds of even oil companies and governments," said Melchett.

In a dual-pronged strategy, Greenpeace on Wednesday also challenged the British government to divert 17 million sterling from fossil fuel subsidies into a programme to solar power fifty thousand homes.
Solar power has the potential to replace two thirds of British electricity production, said campaigner Jane Wildblood.
"British politicians still seem to think that solar technology won't work in Britain. It does. It works all year round, in summer and winter, even in the rain," she said.
